analysis:
Examined all five changed files. The changes are limited to diagnostics and CLI status rendering.

StartupPreloader.swift adds two summary fields, `failedInsufficientMemory` and `notAttempted`, and records them at lines 159-162 and 203-206. The memory-admission logic is unchanged, so it still never evicts. No new I/O, crypto, authorization or network behavior was added, and the closed-category public-log convention is unchanged. `isInsufficientMemoryLoad` (lines 259-275) is unchanged.

StatusCommand+Residency.swift adds `pendingSelectionLines` and `recoveryLines`. StatusCommand.swift (lines 151 and 174-176) wires them into `printDaemonStatus`. They only read the owner-only daemon state file written by the same-user daemon and print to the local terminal. The new inputs are `enabledModelsAtStart`, `enabledModelsAtLastSwitch` and `selectedModelRecovery` (model, blocker, timings). The blocker string contains model IDs and memory figures, and it goes only to the operator's own stdout. It is not sent to the coordinator or public logs in this diff. That is consistent with the T-058 and onInsufficientMemory convention that detailed values stay in owner-only state and diagnostics. The same-UID attacker model (TB-003) already allows state-file tampering. The worst result is misleading status text, with no authorization effect.

An unrelated enabledModels mismatch is only displayed. It does not influence serving authorization (A-016), attestation, key custody or prefix-cache behavior (T-041), so no threat IDs are affected.

The test file only adds status-output tests inside a sandbox.

Remaining integration question: where the daemon populates `selected_model_recovery` and `enabled_models_at_*` is not in the supplied evidence, so I cannot check whether it redacts blockers or sanitizes the strings. Control characters in model IDs or blockers from a tampered state file could reach the terminal. That is a low-impact, same-user concern.
